This guide describes secure authorization and access-control patterns for Soroban smart contracts. It covers common patterns (role-based, capability-based), where to place checks, insecure anti-patterns, and guidance for testing authorization paths. Prerequisites Rust and cargo Soroban CLI and soroban_sdk Familiarity with Address and require_auth() semantics Goals Make authorization checks explicit and auditable. Keep capability boundaries small and verifiable. Prefer least-privilege defaults and fail-safe behavior. Patterns Role-based access​ Store a small, explicit mapping from an Address to role identifiers. Check role membership at the edge of functions that modify sensitive state. See the tested access-control example for a complete role-based access control (RBAC) implementation: a Role enum (Admin, Manager, User), role assignments held in env.storage().persistent(), and a reusable has_role/require_role check used to guard restricted entry points. Capability-based access​ Give callers limited capabilities (tokens, allowances, or dedicated contract entries) instead of broad, single-administrator accounts. Capabilities can be revoked or rotated without changing primary keys. Check early, check often​ Perform authorization checks at public entry points (before expensive work) and re-check invariants when crossing capability boundaries. Principle of least privilege​ Keep privileged operations narrow and minimize the number of privileged addresses or capabilities. Contract Contract (Secure) Tests Insecure: implicit or scattered checks​ #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, Env, Address}; #[contract] pub struct Bad; #[contractimpl] impl Bad { // Uses a single global flag and scattered checks — easy to misuse or forget. pub fn set_admin(env: Env, admin: Address) { // No access control here — anyone can call env.storage().persistent().set(&"admin", &admin); } pub fn privileged_action(env: Env) { // Check is scattered and easy to omit in other methods let admin: Address = env.storage().persistent().get(&"admin").unwrap(); if !env.invoker().eq(&admin) { panic!("unauthorized"); } // do privileged work } } This pattern fails if initialization is incorrect, or if other methods forget the check. Secure: explicit role mapping and require_auth()​ #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, Address, Env}; #[contract] pub struct AccessControl; #[contractimpl] impl AccessControl { pub fn initialize(env: Env, owner: Address) { // initialization should be controlled (callable only once in practice) env.storage().persistent().set(&"owner", &owner); } fn owner_of(env: &Env) -> Address { env.storage().persistent().get(&"owner").unwrap() } pub fn set_admin(env: Env, admin: Address) { // Require the owner to sign before changing admin let owner = Self::owner_of(&env); owner.require_auth(); env.storage().persistent().set(&"admin", &admin); } pub fn privileged_action(env: Env) { let admin: Address = env.storage().persistent().get(&"admin").unwrap(); admin.require_auth(); // safely perform privileged work } } Key points: Use Address::require_auth() to assert caller identity. Keep mapping keys explicit and minimal (owner, admin, or a small role map). Prefer dedicated setter methods guarded by the highest privilege. #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::{testutils::Address as _, Env}; #[test] fn test_admin_flow() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, AccessControl); let client = AccessControlClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let owner = Address::generate(&env); let alice = Address::generate(&env); env.mock_all_auths(); // Initialize and set admin client.initialize(&owner); env.set_source_account(&owner); client.set_admin(&alice); // Admin action must be signed by admin env.set_source_account(&alice); client.privileged_action(); } } Anti-patterns Relying on env.invoker() checks scattered throughout code without enforcing signing (require_auth is safer). Granting a single address unlimited rights without revocation or rotation plan. Mixing business logic and authorization checks in many places instead of centralizing them. Testing Authorization Paths Unit tests: assert both authorized and unauthorized callers for every public method. Edge cases: test initialization, role rotation, and revocation flows. Property/fuzz testing: ensure that random inputs cannot bypass checks. Use env.mock_all_auths() carefully to ensure you still assert require_auth() behavior where relevant. Audit and Review Keep the role map small and well-documented. Document the capability boundaries in the contract README. Consider off-chain governance flows for role changes. Further reading Core concepts: see the Authorization concept page for signer primitives and examples. Security Fundamentals — access control checklist

This pattern demonstrates a complete basic token contract implementing three core operations: mint, transfer, and balance. It serves as the foundation for understanding token mechanics in Soroban before advancing to standardized token interfaces like SAC (Soroban Asset Contract). When to use Use this pattern to bootstrap a simple token system, understand state management for balances, and grasp authorization patterns. For production, consider using SAC or wrapping existing assets. Prerequisites Rust stable and cargo Soroban CLI installed (setup guide) Basic familiarity with Soroban contracts and the soroban_sdk Understanding of Address types and authentication Implementation The contract manages a ledger mapping addresses to token balances using persistent storage. Three public functions allow minting tokens, querying balances, and transferring between accounts. Contract Running Tests #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contracterror, contractimpl, contracttype, Address, Env}; /// Storage key for tracking token balances per address. #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone)] pub enum DataKey { Balance(Address), } /// Error codes for token operations. #[contracterror] #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Ord)] #[repr(u32)] pub enum Error { InsufficientBalance = 1, InvalidAmount = 2, SelfTransfer = 3, } #[contract] pub struct TokenTransfer; #[contractimpl] impl TokenTransfer { /// Mint tokens to an address (for testing and bootstrapping). /// In production, restrict this to authorized minters. pub fn mint(env: Env, to: Address, amount: i128) { let key = DataKey::Balance(to.clone()); let current: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&key).unwrap_or(0); env.storage().persistent().set(&key, &(current + amount)); } /// Query the token balance of an address. pub fn balance(env: Env, of: Address) -> i128 { let key = DataKey::Balance(of); env.storage().persistent().get(&key).unwrap_or(0) } /// Transfer tokens from sender to recipient. /// Requires authorization from the sender address. pub fn transfer(env: Env, from: Address, to: Address, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error> { from.require_auth(); // Validate amount if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } // Prevent self-transfer if from == to { return Err(Error::SelfTransfer); } // Check sender has sufficient balance let from_key = DataKey::Balance(from.clone()); let from_balance: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&from_key).unwrap_or(0); if from_balance < amount { return Err(Error::InsufficientBalance); } // Perform transfer let to_key = DataKey::Balance(to.clone()); let to_balance: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&to_key).unwrap_or(0); env.storage() .persistent() .set(&from_key, &(from_balance - amount)); env.storage() .persistent() .set(&to_key, &(to_balance + amount)); Ok(()) } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::{testutils::Address as _, Env}; fn setup() -> (Env, TokenTransferClient<'static>) { let env = Env::default(); env.mock_all_auths(); let contract_id = env.register(TokenTransfer, ()); let client = TokenTransferClient::new(&env, &contract_id); (env, client) } #[test] fn test_mint_increases_balance() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); client.mint(&alice, &500); assert_eq!(client.balance(&alice), 500); } #[test] fn test_transfer_moves_tokens() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); client.mint(&alice, &1000); client.transfer(&alice, &bob, &400); assert_eq!(client.balance(&alice), 600); assert_eq!(client.balance(&bob), 400); } #[test] fn test_transfer_fails_on_insufficient_balance() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); client.mint(&alice, &100); let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &200); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InsufficientBalance))); assert_eq!(client.balance(&alice), 100); assert_eq!(client.balance(&bob), 0); } #[test] fn test_transfer_fails_on_invalid_amount() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); client.mint(&alice, &100); let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &0); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InvalidAmount))); let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &-50); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InvalidAmount))); } #[test] fn test_self_transfer_is_rejected() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); client.mint(&alice, &100); let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &alice, &50); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::SelfTransfer))); } #[test] fn test_initial_balance_is_zero() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); assert_eq!(client.balance(&alice), 0); } } Run the example tests to verify the implementation: cd examples/token-transfer cargo test Expected output: 6 passing tests covering mint, transfer, balance, validation, and edge cases. Key Concepts Storage Model​ Balances are stored in persistent storage using the Balance(Address) enum variant as the key. This allows efficient lookups and updates without scanning the entire ledger. Authorization​ The transfer function calls from.require_auth() to ensure the transaction is signed by the sender. This prevents unauthorized token transfers. Error Handling​ Three error codes cover the main failure modes: InsufficientBalance: Sender doesn't have enough tokens InvalidAmount: Zero or negative amounts are rejected SelfTransfer: Transferring to yourself is a no-op and disallowed Minting​ The mint function bypasses authorization checks. In production, restrict minting to authorized parties using a minter role or ownership model. Security Considerations Unrestricted Minting: The current implementation allows anyone to mint tokens. Add access control using an admin address or authorized minters list before production use. No Decimal Support: This basic implementation uses integers only. For real assets, consider implementing a decimals field and decimal-aware math. Supply Cap: Consider implementing a maximum supply to prevent unlimited inflation. Allowance/Approval: For more advanced use cases, implement an approve/transferFrom pattern allowing third parties to move tokens on behalf of the owner. Comparison: Basic Token vs. SAC Feature Basic Token SAC (Stellar Asset Contract) Standards Custom Soroban standard Decimals Built-in only Full decimal support Approvals Not included Built-in allowances Admin None Admin actions (freeze, clawback) Production Ready No Yes Learning Value High N/A For production systems, use SAC. This pattern is ideal for learning and prototyping. Deploy to Testnet​ Generate or use an existing account: soroban keys generate token-admin Fund your account via the Stellar Testnet Faucet. Deploy the contract: soroban contract deploy \ --wasm target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/token_transfer.wasm \ --network testnet \ --source token-admin This returns a contract ID (e.g., CABC...). Interact with the contract: soroban contract invoke \ --id CABC... \ --network testnet \ --source token-admin \ -- mint \ --to $(soroban keys address token-admin) \ --amount 1000 Query Balance​ soroban contract invoke \ --id CABC... \ --network testnet \ --source token-admin \ -- balance \ --of $(soroban keys address token-admin) Transfer Tokens​ soroban contract invoke \ --id CABC... \ --network testnet \ --source token-admin \ -- transfer \ --from $(soroban keys address token-admin) \ --to GBBD...your-recipient \ --amount 100 For more details, see the Deploy to Testnet guide.

The contract factory pattern enables dynamic deployment of multiple contract instances from a single factory contract. This is useful for creating standardized contracts at runtime without manual deployment.

A factory contract acts as a centralized deployer that can: Deploy child contract instances on-demand Track all deployed instances Initialize child contracts with custom parameters Manage the lifecycle of multiple contracts

Token Issuance: Deploy a new token contract for each asset User Accounts: Create individual contract instances for user-specific logic Multi-tenancy: Deploy isolated instances for different organizations Pool Management: Create liquidity pools dynamically Marketplace: Deploy individual shop contracts from a marketplace factory

The factory pattern typically consists of: Factory Contract: Manages deployment and tracking Child Contract: The template contract that gets deployed multiple times Registry: Maintains a list of deployed instances Factory Contract ├── deploy_child(name) ├── get_deployed_children() └── child_count() Child Contract (Template) ├── init(name) ├── get_name() └── get_info()

The child contract is the template that will be deployed multiple times: #[contract] pub struct ChildContract; #[contractimpl] impl ChildContract { pub fn init(env: Env, name: Symbol) { env.storage().instance().set(&symbol_short!("name"), &name); } pub fn get_name(env: Env) -> Symbol { env.storage() .instance() .get(&symbol_short!("name")) .unwrap_or(Symbol::new(&env, "unnamed")) } pub fn get_info(env: Env) -> (Symbol, Address) { let name = env .storage() .instance() .get(&symbol_short!("name")) .unwrap_or(Symbol::new(&env, "unnamed")); let contract_id = env.current_contract_address(); (name, contract_id) } }

The factory deploys and tracks child instances: #[contract] pub struct ContractFactory; #[contractimpl] impl ContractFactory { pub fn deploy_child(env: Env, name: Symbol) -> Address { // Get child contract code let child_code = env.deployer().get_programm_id(&symbol_short!("child")); // Generate unique salt for deterministic deployment let salt = env.storage().temporary().get::<(), u64>(&()).unwrap_or(0); env.storage() .temporary() .set(&(), &(salt + 1)); let salt_bytes = salt.to_le_bytes().to_vec(); // Deploy new instance let child_address = env .deployer() .deploy_contract( &salt_bytes, &child_code, Address::from_contract_id(&env.current_contract_address()) ); // Track deployed contract let mut deployed: Vec<Address> = env .storage() .persistent() .get(&symbol_short!("deployed")) .unwrap_or_else(|| vec![&env]); deployed.push_back(child_address.clone()); env.storage() .persistent() .set(&symbol_short!("deployed"), &deployed); child_address } pub fn get_deployed_children(env: Env) -> Vec<Address> { env.storage() .persistent() .get(&symbol_short!("deployed")) .unwrap_or_else(|| vec![&env]) } pub fn child_count(env: Env) -> u32 { let deployed: Vec<Address> = env .storage() .persistent() .get(&symbol_short!("deployed")) .unwrap_or_else(|| vec![&env]); deployed.len() as u32 } }

The factory pattern includes comprehensive tests: #[test] fn test_factory_deploy_multiple_children() { let env = Env::default(); let factory_contract_id = env.register_contract(None, ContractFactory); let factory_client = ContractFactoryClient::new(&env, &factory_contract_id); // Deploy multiple children let child1 = factory_client.deploy_child(&Symbol::new(&env, "child-1")); let child2 = factory_client.deploy_child(&Symbol::new(&env, "child-2")); let child3 = factory_client.deploy_child(&Symbol::new(&env, "child-3")); // Verify all are tracked assert_eq!(factory_client.child_count(), 3); let deployed = factory_client.get_deployed_children(); assert_eq!(deployed.len(), 3); assert!(deployed.contains(&child1)); assert!(deployed.contains(&child2)); assert!(deployed.contains(&child3)); }
Use unique salts to ensure different deployment addresses: let salt = env.storage().temporary().get::<(), u64>(&()).unwrap_or(0); let salt_bytes = salt.to_le_bytes().to_vec();
Persistent storage: For tracking important metadata Temporary storage: For non-critical counters Instance storage: For child contract-specific data
Always initialize child contracts with necessary parameters: client.init(&name);
Maintain a registry of deployed instances for: Verification Monitoring Upgrade coordination Access control

Pass parameters when deploying: pub fn deploy_child_with_params( env: Env, name: Symbol, owner: Address, config: Config, ) -> Address { // Deploy let child_address = /* deployment logic */; // Initialize with parameters let client = ChildContractClient::new(&env, &child_address); client.init(&name); // ... set owner, config, etc child_address }

Restrict who can deploy: pub fn deploy_child(env: Env, name: Symbol) -> Address { let caller = env.invoker(); let authorized: Address = env.storage() .persistent() .get(&symbol_short!("admin")) .expect("Admin not set"); require_auth(&caller); require!(caller == authorized, Error::NotAuthorized); // Deploy logic... }

Retrieve specific child contracts: pub fn get_child_by_index(env: Env, index: u32) -> Address { let deployed: Vec<Address> = env .storage() .persistent() .get(&symbol_short!("deployed")) .unwrap_or_else(|| vec![&env]); deployed.get(index as usize) }

Unique Salts: Ensure each deployment uses a unique salt Initialization: Always initialize child contracts properly Tracking: Maintain a registry of deployed instances Access Control: Restrict deployment permissions if needed Testing: Test deployment, tracking, and retrieval Documentation: Document child contract interfaces clearly

In Soroban, types are more than just data containers—they define the contract's storage footprint, gas efficiency, and long-term maintainability. This guide covers strategies for designing custom types that are robust, efficient, and evolvable. Why Type Design Matters Smart contracts are immutable by nature, but their state persists across upgrades. Poorly designed types can lead to "storage bloat," high gas costs for reads/writes, and complex migrations when business requirements change.
When translating domain concepts (like "User Account" or "Liquidity Pool") into contract types, you must decide how to represent them in storage.

Value Objects: Types defined by their attributes (e.g., Amount, Price). In Soroban, these are usually small structs or newtype wrappers. Entities: Types with a unique identity that persists over time (e.g., User, Proposal). These are typically stored as large structs keyed by a unique ID or Address.

Use the "Newtype" pattern to wrap primitive types. This prevents accidental confusion between different units or IDs that share the same underlying type. #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub struct OrderId(pub u32); #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub struct TokenId(pub u32); // Compiler will prevent passing a TokenId where an OrderId is expected pub fn get_order(env: Env, id: OrderId) { ... }
Soroban uses a highly optimized serialization format (XDR). To make a custom type usable in a contract, it must be annotated with #[contracttype].

Structs: For grouping related data. Enums: For representing state or mutually exclusive options. Prims: i128, u32, Address, Bytes, Symbol, etc. #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum ContractState { Active, Paused, Upgrading(u32), // Enums can carry data } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub struct Order { pub id: OrderId, pub owner: Address, pub amount: i128, pub status: ContractState, }
Every byte stored in the ledger costs gas. Serialization size directly impacts the read_ledger_entry and write_ledger_entry costs.

Prefer Small Primitives: Use u32 or u64 instead of i128 if the value range allows. Avoid Unnecessary Strings: Use Symbol for short, fixed strings (up to 32 characters). They are significantly cheaper than String. Flat vs. Nested: Highly nested structs increase serialization complexity. Keep storage types as flat as possible. Bit-Packing (Advanced): For extremely high-frequency operations, consider packing multiple booleans or small integers into a single u64. Read/Write Amplification Reading a 1KB struct to change a single boolean field still costs the gas for a 1KB read. If a struct grows too large, consider splitting it into separate storage keys.

Use enums to manage the lifecycle of a contract or entity. This makes illegal transitions impossible at the type level. #[contracttype] pub enum ProposalStatus { Pending, Voting { start_time: u64, end_time: u64 }, Executed, Expired, } pub fn cast_vote(env: Env, id: u32) -> Result<(), Error> { let proposal = get_proposal(&env, id)?; match proposal.status { ProposalStatus::Voting { start_time, end_time } => { let now = env.ledger().timestamp(); if now < start_time || now > end_time { return Err(Error::VotingNotActive); } // Proceed with voting... } _ => return Err(Error::InvalidStatus), } Ok(()) }

Group global contract settings into a single struct. This is more efficient than storing 10 separate configuration variables in 10 different storage keys. #[contracttype] pub struct Config { pub admin: Address, pub fee_bps: u32, pub min_deposit: i128, } impl Config { pub fn get(env: &Env) -> Self { env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Config).unwrap() } }
Never trust data coming into the contract. Validate types at the entry point (contractimpl).

Range Checks: Ensure amounts are positive and within expected bounds. Sanitization: Check that Address types aren't the null address if applicable. State Invariants: Verify that the internal state of a struct is consistent (e.g., start_time < end_time). pub fn create_order(env: Env, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error> { if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } // ... }
As your project grows, you may need to add fields to your structs. Because storage is persistent, you must handle "schema drift."

Instead of storing a raw struct, store an enum that wraps different versions of the data. #[contracttype] pub enum AccountState { V1(AccountV1), V2(AccountV2), } #[contracttype] pub struct AccountV1 { pub balance: i128, } #[contracttype] pub struct AccountV2 { pub balance: i128, pub rewards_points: u64, // New field added in V2 } // Lazy Migration pub fn get_account(env: &Env, user: Address) -> AccountV2 { let state: AccountState = env.storage().persistent().get(&user).unwrap(); match state { AccountState::V1(v1) => { // Upgrade V1 to V2 on the fly AccountV2 { balance: v1.balance, rewards_points: 0, } } AccountState::V2(v2) => v2, } }

Integer Overflows: Always use checked math (checked_add, checked_mul) when performing calculations on numeric types. Unbounded Collections: Avoid using Vec or Map in storage types if they can grow indefinitely. This can lead to "gas exhaustion" attacks where reading the state becomes impossible. Type Confusion: Use Symbol or OrderId wrappers to ensure you aren't using a user-provided integer to index into the wrong data structure.

All custom types are annotated with #[contracttype]. Enums are used to represent state and avoid "boolean soup." Newtype wrappers protect against ID/unit confusion. Large structs are evaluated for potential splitting to save gas. A migration strategy (like Versioned State) is planned for future updates. Inputs are validated at the contract boundary.

This pattern guide defines a comprehensive error handling methodology for Soroban smart contracts. It covers establishing a clear error taxonomy, implementing custom error patterns, executing propagation strategies, and ensuring user-facing clarity. Prerequisites Rust stable and cargo Soroban CLI installed Basic understanding of Rust's Result type and enum definitions Familiarity with the soroban_sdk environment Error Taxonomy and Custom Patterns A well-defined error taxonomy categorizes errors into logical groups. This prevents overlapping error codes, aids debugging, and makes client-side handling predictable. Common Taxonomy Categories​ Validation Errors (100-199): Invalid inputs, out of bounds, incorrect formats. Authorization Errors (200-299): Missing signatures, unauthorized roles. State Errors (300-399): Invalid state transitions, uninitialized data. Resource Errors (400-499): Insufficient balance, out of gas. Contract Test #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, contracttype, Env, Address}; #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum Error { // Validation Errors (100+) InvalidAmount = 101, InvalidAddress = 102, // Authorization Errors (200+) Unauthorized = 201, RoleNotFound = 202, // State Errors (300+) AlreadyInitialized = 301, NotInitialized = 302, // Resource Errors (400+) InsufficientBalance = 401, InsufficientAllowance = 402, } #[contract] pub struct TokenContract; #[contractimpl] impl TokenContract { pub fn transfer( env: Env, from: Address, to: Address, amount: i128, ) -> Result<(), Error> { from.require_auth(); if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } let balance = env.storage().persistent().get(&from).unwrap_or(0); if balance < amount { return Err(Error::InsufficientBalance); } // Execute transfer logic here (simplified for example) let new_balance = balance - amount; env.storage().persistent().set(&from, &new_balance); Ok(()) } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::{testutils::Address as _, Env}; #[test] fn test_taxonomy_errors() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, TokenContract); let client = TokenContractClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); env.mock_all_auths(); // Test Validation Error (100-199 range) let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &-10); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InvalidAmount))); // Test Resource Error (400-499 range) let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &100); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InsufficientBalance))); } } Propagation and Handling Strategies Using the ? operator allows you to gracefully propagate errors up the call stack. This pattern advocates breaking complex operations into smaller, isolated functions that validate conditions or calculate state and return a Result. Why Propagate? Propagating errors rather than panicking ensures that your contract gracefully halts and provides exact error reasons to the caller, preventing unknown execution states. Contract Test #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, Env, Address}; #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum WorkflowError { InvalidInput = 1, ProcessingFailed = 2, } #[contract] pub struct WorkflowContract; #[contractimpl] impl WorkflowContract { pub fn complex_workflow(env: Env, user: Address, value: i128) -> Result<(), WorkflowError> { user.require_auth(); // Strategy: Delegate and propagate errors using '?' Self::validate_input(&env, value)?; Self::process_data(&env, &user, value)?; Ok(()) } fn validate_input(_env: &Env, value: i128) -> Result<(), WorkflowError> { if value < 0 { return Err(WorkflowError::InvalidInput); } Ok(()) } fn process_data(env: &Env, user: &Address, value: i128) -> Result<(), WorkflowError> { // Business logic that could fail if value == 42 { return Err(WorkflowError::ProcessingFailed); } env.storage().persistent().set(user, &value); Ok(()) } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::{testutils::Address as _, Env}; #[test] fn test_error_propagation() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, WorkflowContract); let client = WorkflowContractClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let user = Address::generate(&env); env.mock_all_auths(); // The error naturally propagates from validate_input up to the contract entrypoint let result_validation = client.try_complex_workflow(&user, &-5); assert_eq!(result_validation, Err(Ok(WorkflowError::InvalidInput))); // The error propagates from process_data up to the contract entrypoint let result_processing = client.try_complex_workflow(&user, &42); assert_eq!(result_processing, Err(Ok(WorkflowError::ProcessingFailed))); } } User-Facing Clarity Recommendations To ensure frontend clients and indexers can clearly interpret contract failures, implement these recommendations: Standardize Error Codes: Publicly document your error taxonomy in your repository (e.g., in a README or developer portal). Clients rely on these numerical codes. Emit Telemetry Events: For critical path failures, emit an event before returning an error. This aids indexing services in tracking exact failure reasons. Use Descriptive Enums: Naming your Rust enum variants clearly translates to easier debugging when using the Soroban CLI or SDK tools. Provide Client-Side Mapping: Create an SDK or frontend utility mapping the numeric u32 error codes to human-readable messages (e.g., 101 -> "The requested token amount is invalid"). Event Emission on Failure Remember that if a contract returns an error, the transaction rolls back, and any events emitted during that invocation are dropped. Therefore, telemetry events for failures only work if you catch the error at a higher level or in a parent contract. Therefore, telemetry events for failures only work if you catch the error at a higher level or in a parent contract.

Robust error handling is critical for production smart contracts. This guide demonstrates try-catch patterns, fallback logic, graceful degradation, transaction rollback, and comprehensive validation strategies in Soroban. Why Error Recovery Matters Smart contracts handle valuable assets and critical operations. Proper error handling prevents fund loss, ensures predictable behavior, and provides clear feedback when operations fail.
Rust stable and cargo Soroban CLI installed (setup guide) Understanding of Rust's Result type and error handling Familiarity with Soroban SDK error types

Soroban uses Rust's Result type for error handling, which is analogous to try-catch in other languages. Contract Test #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, contracttype, Env, Address, Symbol}; #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum Error { InsufficientBalance = 1, Unauthorized = 2, InvalidAmount = 3, TransferFailed = 4, } #[contract] pub struct TokenContract; #[contractimpl] impl TokenContract { /// Transfer with comprehensive error handling pub fn transfer( env: Env, from: Address, to: Address, amount: i128, ) -> Result<(), Error> { // Validate authorization from.require_auth(); // Validate inputs Self::validate_transfer(&env, &from, &to, amount)?; // Attempt transfer with error handling Self::execute_transfer(&env, &from, &to, amount)?; // Emit success event env.events().publish( (Symbol::new(&env, "transfer"), &from, &to), amount, ); Ok(()) } fn validate_transfer( env: &Env, from: &Address, to: &Address, amount: i128, ) -> Result<(), Error> { // Validate amount is positive if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } // Validate addresses are different if from == to { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } // Check balance let balance = Self::get_balance(env, from); if balance < amount { return Err(Error::InsufficientBalance); } Ok(()) } fn execute_transfer( env: &Env, from: &Address, to: &Address, amount: i128, ) -> Result<(), Error> { let from_balance = Self::get_balance(env, from); let to_balance = Self::get_balance(env, to); // Perform atomic update env.storage().persistent().set(from, &(from_balance - amount)); env.storage().persistent().set(to, &(to_balance + amount)); Ok(()) } fn get_balance(env: &Env, addr: &Address) -> i128 { env.storage() .persistent() .get(addr) .unwrap_or(0) } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::{testutils::Address as _, Env}; #[test] fn test_successful_transfer() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, TokenContract); let client = TokenContractClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); // Setup initial balance env.storage().persistent().set(&alice, &1000_i128); // Execute transfer env.mock_all_auths(); let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &100); assert!(result.is_ok()); assert_eq!(client.get_balance(&alice), 900); assert_eq!(client.get_balance(&bob), 100); } #[test] fn test_insufficient_balance_error() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, TokenContract); let client = TokenContractClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); env.storage().persistent().set(&alice, &50_i128); env.mock_all_auths(); let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &100); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InsufficientBalance))); } #[test] fn test_invalid_amount_error() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, TokenContract); let client = TokenContractClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); env.mock_all_auths(); let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &-100); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InvalidAmount))); } } Best Practice Always use Result<T, Error> return types for functions that can fail. This makes error handling explicit and forces callers to handle potential failures.

Implement fallback mechanisms when primary operations fail. Contract Test #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, Env, Address, Symbol}; #[contract] pub struct PriceOracle; #[contractimpl] impl PriceOracle { /// Get price with fallback to secondary oracle pub fn get_price_with_fallback( env: Env, asset: Symbol, ) -> Result<i128, Error> { // Try primary oracle match Self::get_primary_price(&env, &asset) { Ok(price) => { env.events().publish( (Symbol::new(&env, "price_source"),), Symbol::new(&env, "primary"), ); Ok(price) } Err(_) => { // Fallback to secondary oracle match Self::get_secondary_price(&env, &asset) { Ok(price) => { env.events().publish( (Symbol::new(&env, "price_source"),), Symbol::new(&env, "secondary"), ); Ok(price) } Err(_) => { // Final fallback to cached price Self::get_cached_price(&env, &asset) .ok_or(Error::NoPriceAvailable) } } } } } fn get_primary_price(env: &Env, asset: &Symbol) -> Result<i128, Error> { env.storage() .persistent() .get(&(Symbol::new(env, "primary"), asset)) .ok_or(Error::PrimaryOracleFailed) } fn get_secondary_price(env: &Env, asset: &Symbol) -> Result<i128, Error> { env.storage() .persistent() .get(&(Symbol::new(env, "secondary"), asset)) .ok_or(Error::SecondaryOracleFailed) } fn get_cached_price(env: &Env, asset: &Symbol) -> Option<i128> { env.storage() .temporary() .get(&(Symbol::new(env, "cache"), asset)) } } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum Error { PrimaryOracleFailed = 1, SecondaryOracleFailed = 2, NoPriceAvailable = 3, } #[test] fn test_fallback_to_secondary() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, PriceOracle); let client = PriceOracleClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let asset = Symbol::new(&env, "XLM"); // Primary fails, secondary succeeds env.storage().persistent().set( &(Symbol::new(&env, "secondary"), &asset), &100_i128, ); let price = client.get_price_with_fallback(&asset); assert_eq!(price, Ok(100)); } #[test] fn test_fallback_to_cache() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, PriceOracle); let client = PriceOracleClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let asset = Symbol::new(&env, "XLM"); // Both oracles fail, use cache env.storage().temporary().set( &(Symbol::new(&env, "cache"), &asset), &95_i128, ); let price = client.get_price_with_fallback(&asset); assert_eq!(price, Ok(95)); } Fallback Considerations Ensure fallback data sources are reliable and up-to-date. Stale cached data can lead to incorrect contract behavior.

Design contracts to continue operating with reduced functionality when errors occur. Contract Test #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, Env, Address, Symbol}; #[contract] pub struct DexContract; #[contractimpl] impl DexContract { /// Swap with graceful degradation pub fn swap_with_degradation( env: Env, user: Address, amount_in: i128, min_amount_out: i128, ) -> Result<SwapResult, Error> { user.require_auth(); // Try optimal routing match Self::try_optimal_swap(&env, &user, amount_in, min_amount_out) { Ok(result) => Ok(result), Err(Error::OptimalRouteFailed) => { // Degrade to direct swap env.events().publish( (Symbol::new(&env, "degraded_mode"),), Symbol::new(&env, "direct_swap"), ); Self::try_direct_swap(&env, &user, amount_in, min_amount_out) } Err(e) => Err(e), } } fn try_optimal_swap( env: &Env, user: &Address, amount_in: i128, min_amount_out: i128, ) -> Result<SwapResult, Error> { // Complex multi-hop routing let route = Self::calculate_optimal_route(env, amount_in)?; Self::execute_multi_hop_swap(env, user, &route, min_amount_out) } fn try_direct_swap( env: &Env, user: &Address, amount_in: i128, min_amount_out: i128, ) -> Result<SwapResult, Error> { // Simple direct pool swap let amount_out = Self::calculate_direct_swap(env, amount_in)?; if amount_out < min_amount_out { return Err(Error::SlippageTooHigh); } Self::execute_direct_swap(env, user, amount_in, amount_out) } fn calculate_optimal_route( env: &Env, amount_in: i128, ) -> Result<Vec<Address>, Error> { // Simulate route calculation that might fail env.storage() .temporary() .get(&Symbol::new(env, "route")) .ok_or(Error::OptimalRouteFailed) } fn execute_multi_hop_swap( env: &Env, user: &Address, route: &Vec<Address>, min_amount_out: i128, ) -> Result<SwapResult, Error> { // Execute complex swap Ok(SwapResult { amount_out: 1000, route_type: Symbol::new(env, "optimal"), }) } fn calculate_direct_swap(env: &Env, amount_in: i128) -> Result<i128, Error> { // Simple calculation Ok(amount_in * 95 / 100) // 5% slippage } fn execute_direct_swap( env: &Env, user: &Address, amount_in: i128, amount_out: i128, ) -> Result<SwapResult, Error> { Ok(SwapResult { amount_out, route_type: Symbol::new(env, "direct"), }) } } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub struct SwapResult { pub amount_out: i128, pub route_type: Symbol, } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum Error { OptimalRouteFailed = 1, SlippageTooHigh = 2, InsufficientLiquidity = 3, } #[test] fn test_graceful_degradation() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, DexContract); let client = DexContractClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let user = Address::generate(&env); // Optimal route not available, should degrade to direct env.mock_all_auths(); let result = client.swap_with_degradation(&user, &1000, &900); assert!(result.is_ok()); let swap_result = result.unwrap(); assert_eq!(swap_result.route_type, Symbol::new(&env, "direct")); } Graceful Degradation Benefits Graceful degradation ensures your contract remains functional even when optimal paths fail, improving reliability and user experience.

Soroban automatically rolls back state changes when a contract panics or returns an error. Contract Test #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, Env, Address}; #[contract] pub struct AtomicSwap; #[contractimpl] impl AtomicSwap { /// Atomic swap - all or nothing pub fn atomic_swap( env: Env, user_a: Address, user_b: Address, amount_a: i128, amount_b: i128, ) -> Result<(), Error> { user_a.require_auth(); user_b.require_auth(); // All operations succeed or all fail (automatic rollback) Self::validate_balances(&env, &user_a, &user_b, amount_a, amount_b)?; Self::execute_swap(&env, &user_a, &user_b, amount_a, amount_b)?; Self::emit_swap_event(&env, &user_a, &user_b, amount_a, amount_b); Ok(()) } fn validate_balances( env: &Env, user_a: &Address, user_b: &Address, amount_a: i128, amount_b: i128, ) -> Result<(), Error> { let balance_a = Self::get_balance(env, user_a); let balance_b = Self::get_balance(env, user_b); if balance_a < amount_a { // This error causes automatic rollback return Err(Error::InsufficientBalanceA); } if balance_b < amount_b { // This error causes automatic rollback return Err(Error::InsufficientBalanceB); } Ok(()) } fn execute_swap( env: &Env, user_a: &Address, user_b: &Address, amount_a: i128, amount_b: i128, ) -> Result<(), Error> { // These changes are atomic - all succeed or all rollback let balance_a = Self::get_balance(env, user_a); let balance_b = Self::get_balance(env, user_b); env.storage().persistent().set(user_a, &(balance_a - amount_a + amount_b)); env.storage().persistent().set(user_b, &(balance_b - amount_b + amount_a)); Ok(()) } fn emit_swap_event( env: &Env, user_a: &Address, user_b: &Address, amount_a: i128, amount_b: i128, ) { env.events().publish( (Symbol::new(env, "swap"), user_a, user_b), (amount_a, amount_b), ); } fn get_balance(env: &Env, addr: &Address) -> i128 { env.storage().persistent().get(addr).unwrap_or(0) } } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum Error { InsufficientBalanceA = 1, InsufficientBalanceB = 2, } #[test] fn test_rollback_on_error() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, AtomicSwap); let client = AtomicSwapClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); // Setup: Alice has 100, Bob has 50 env.storage().persistent().set(&alice, &100_i128); env.storage().persistent().set(&bob, &50_i128); env.mock_all_auths(); // Try to swap more than Bob has - should fail and rollback let result = client.try_atomic_swap(&alice, &bob, &50, &100); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InsufficientBalanceB))); // Verify balances unchanged (rollback worked) assert_eq!(client.get_balance(&alice), 100); assert_eq!(client.get_balance(&bob), 50); } #[test] fn test_successful_atomic_swap() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, AtomicSwap); let client = AtomicSwapClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); env.storage().persistent().set(&alice, &100_i128); env.storage().persistent().set(&bob, &200_i128); env.mock_all_auths(); let result = client.try_atomic_swap(&alice, &bob, &50, &100); assert!(result.is_ok()); assert_eq!(client.get_balance(&alice), 150); // 100 - 50 + 100 assert_eq!(client.get_balance(&bob), 150); // 200 - 100 + 50 } Automatic Rollback Soroban automatically rolls back all state changes when a contract returns an error or panics. You don't need to manually undo changes.

Validate all inputs early to fail fast and provide clear error messages. Contract Test #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, Env, Address, String}; #[contract] pub struct ValidatedContract; #[contractimpl] impl ValidatedContract { pub fn create_order( env: Env, user: Address, amount: i128, price: i128, expiry: u64, ) -> Result<u64, Error> { user.require_auth(); // Comprehensive validation Self::validate_order_params(&env, amount, price, expiry)?; // Execute business logic let order_id = Self::store_order(&env, &user, amount, price, expiry); Ok(order_id) } fn validate_order_params( env: &Env, amount: i128, price: i128, expiry: u64, ) -> Result<(), Error> { // Validate amount if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } if amount > 1_000_000_000 { return Err(Error::AmountTooLarge); } // Validate price if price <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidPrice); } // Validate expiry let current_time = env.ledger().timestamp(); if expiry <= current_time { return Err(Error::ExpiryInPast); } let max_expiry = current_time + (30 * 24 * 60 * 60); // 30 days if expiry > max_expiry { return Err(Error::ExpiryTooFar); } Ok(()) } fn store_order( env: &Env, user: &Address, amount: i128, price: i128, expiry: u64, ) -> u64 { let order_id = Self::get_next_order_id(env); env.storage().persistent().set( &order_id, &Order { user: user.clone(), amount, price, expiry, }, ); order_id } fn get_next_order_id(env: &Env) -> u64 { let current: u64 = env.storage() .instance() .get(&Symbol::new(env, "order_id")) .unwrap_or(0); let next = current + 1; env.storage().instance().set(&Symbol::new(env, "order_id"), &next); next } } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub struct Order { pub user: Address, pub amount: i128, pub price: i128, pub expiry: u64, } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum Error { InvalidAmount = 1, AmountTooLarge = 2, InvalidPrice = 3, ExpiryInPast = 4, ExpiryTooFar = 5, } #[test] fn test_validation_invalid_amount() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, ValidatedContract); let client = ValidatedContractClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let user = Address::generate(&env); let expiry = env.ledger().timestamp() + 3600; env.mock_all_auths(); // Test negative amount let result = client.try_create_order(&user, &-100, &1000, &expiry); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InvalidAmount))); // Test zero amount let result = client.try_create_order(&user, &0, &1000, &expiry); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InvalidAmount))); // Test amount too large let result = client.try_create_order(&user, &2_000_000_000, &1000, &expiry); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::AmountTooLarge))); } #[test] fn test_validation_expiry() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, ValidatedContract); let client = ValidatedContractClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let user = Address::generate(&env); let current_time = env.ledger().timestamp(); env.mock_all_auths(); // Test expiry in past let result = client.try_create_order(&user, &100, &1000, &(current_time - 1)); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::ExpiryInPast))); // Test expiry too far let far_future = current_time + (60 * 24 * 60 * 60); // 60 days let result = client.try_create_order(&user, &100, &1000, &far_future); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::ExpiryTooFar))); } Validation Best Practices Validate all inputs at function entry - Provide specific error types for different validation failures - Check business logic constraints (ranges, relationships) - Validate time-based parameters against ledger time

Critical Security Practices Never ignore errors: Always handle Result types explicitly Validate before state changes: Check all conditions before modifying storage Use specific error types: Avoid generic errors that hide root causes Test error paths: Write tests for every error condition Avoid panics in production: Use Result instead of panic! or unwrap()

// ❌ BAD: Ignoring errors let balance = env.storage().get(&user).unwrap(); // Can panic! // ✅ GOOD: Handling errors let balance = env.storage() .get(&user) .unwrap_or(0); // Safe default // ❌ BAD: Generic errors return Err(Error::Failed); // ✅ GOOD: Specific errors return Err(Error::InsufficientBalance); // ❌ BAD: State change before validation env.storage().set(&user, &new_balance); if new_balance < 0 { return Err(Error::Invalid); // Too late! } // ✅ GOOD: Validation before state change if new_balance < 0 { return Err(Error::Invalid); } env.storage().set(&user, &new_balance);

Before deploying your contract, verify: All functions that can fail return Result<T, Error> Custom error enum with specific error types Input validation at function entry No unwrap() or expect() calls in production code Fallback logic for external dependencies Comprehensive error tests Clear error messages in documentation Events emitted for important errors Graceful degradation where appropriate Atomic operations for multi-step processes

In the world of immutable ledgers, contract upgrades are among the most sensitive operations a developer can perform. A mistake in an upgrade can result in permanent loss of state, locked funds, or protocol insolvency. This guide treats contract upgrades as high-risk, irreversible operations requiring rigorous governance and verification. Safety First Always simulate upgrades and migrations on a local sandbox or testnet before executing on mainnet. Once state is corrupted on-chain, recovery is often impossible.
A healthy protocol moves through distinct phases, each with specific entry and exit criteria.
Criteria: Code is feature-complete and passes all unit/integration tests. Action: Internal or external security audit of the Wasm bytecode and source logic. Exit: No high-severity issues remain.

Criteria: Deployment of the exact audited bytecode to a live network environment. Action: Manual QA, integration testing with front-end, and "chaos testing" (e.g., simulating high load). Exit: Contract behaves as expected in a multi-user environment.
Criteria: Final verification of initialization arguments and governance keys. Action: Atomic deployment and initialization. Exit: Success events emitted; state invariants verified.
Criteria: Ongoing operation. Action: Monitoring events, transaction volume, and potential anomalies. Exit: Identification of a bug or requirement for a feature upgrade.

Criteria: A newer version is ready or the feature is sunset. Action: "Sunset" phase where new deposits are disabled but withdrawals remain open. Exit: All funds removed; storage entries deleted where possible.

Upgrades must be protected by strict access control. In Soroban, the upgrade function should typically require the authorization of an admin or a decentralized governance body. #[contractimpl] impl MyContract { pub fn upgrade(env: Env, new_wasm_hash: BytesN<32>) { let admin: Address = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Admin).unwrap(); admin.require_auth(); // Ensure only the authorized admin can upgrade env.deployer().update_current_contract_wasm(new_wasm_hash); } } Governance Best Practice For high-value protocols, avoid single-key admin accounts. Use a multi-signature account or a DAO with a mandatory timelock (e.g., 7 days) to allow users to exit if they disagree with a pending upgrade.
Soroban provides native support for updating contract logic while preserving the contract ID and storage.

The most common way to upgrade is to call env.deployer().update_current_contract_wasm(). This replaces the contract's executable code with the bytecode associated with the provided Wasm hash. Use when: You need to fix a bug or add features without changing the contract's address. Avoid when: You need to change the fundamental architecture or storage model in a way that is incompatible with existing state. See the tested upgradeable example for a complete admin-gated upgrade flow with storage preservation and integration tests.
When you upgrade logic, you often need to evolve the data structures in storage.

Upgrade individual storage entries only when they are accessed. This spreads the gas cost over many transactions and avoids hitting gas limits. #[contracttype] pub enum AccountState { V1(AccountV1), V2(AccountV2), } pub fn get_account_v2(env: &Env, user: Address) -> AccountV2 { let state: AccountState = env.storage().persistent().get(&user).unwrap(); match state { AccountState::V1(v1) => { let upgraded = AccountV2 { balance: v1.balance, rewards: 0, // Initialize new field }; // Save the upgraded state back to storage env.storage().persistent().set(&user, &AccountState::V2(upgraded.clone())); upgraded } AccountState::V2(v2) => v2, } }

Perform the entire migration in a single transaction or a series of transactions. Risk: High gas consumption. May fail if the dataset is too large. Best for: Small, fixed-size datasets (e.g., global configuration).

Bytecode hash of the new Wasm is verified. New storage types are backward-compatible (or migration is planned). Initialization logic for new fields is tested. Upgrade transaction has been simulated on a Testnet fork. Governance keys are active and accessible.
Smoke tests pass (basic deposits/withdrawals). State invariants remain valid (e.g., Total Supply = sum of Balances). Version markers in storage have been updated. Events are being emitted correctly.

If an upgrade introduces a critical flaw, you must have a plan to recover. Immutable Fallback: If the contract is truly immutable, you cannot upgrade. Your only "rollback" is to deploy a new contract and ask users to migrate. Logic Rollback: Call upgrade again with the hash of the previous stable Wasm bytecode. Emergency Pause: Include a "Circuit Breaker" to halt operations while you diagnose and fix a failed upgrade. See the tested emergency-stop example for a minimal, admin-gated pause()/unpause() implementation with a fail_if_paused guard applied to operational entry points.

I have a clearly defined lifecycle for my contract. My upgrade function is protected by require_auth. I have chosen between Lazy and Eager migration for state changes. I have a verified rollback procedure. I have completed the pre-upgrade checklist on Testnet.

In Soroban, performance isn't just about speed—it's about predictability and cost. Every operation (CPU instructions, memory allocation, and ledger access) consumes resources that are metered and capped. This playbook provides a repeatable, measurable workflow for optimizing your contracts. The Three Pillars of Cost CPU Instructions: The computational complexity of your logic. 2. RAM Usage: The memory peak during execution. 3. Storage (Footprint): The size and frequency of ledger reads and writes.

Optimization should never be "blind." Follow this cycle to ensure your efforts are targeted and effective: Measure (Baseline): Use soroban contract simulate to capture current resource usage. Analyze: Identify the bottleneck (e.g., is it high CPU or large storage reads?). Refactor: Apply a specific optimization technique. Verify: Re-measure and compare the delta.

Run your contract function through the CLI simulator to see the raw costs: soroban contract invoke \ --id <CONTRACT_ID> \ --source-account <ACCOUNT> \ --network <NETWORK> \ -- \ <FUNCTION_NAME> \ --arg1 <VALUE> Look for the Events or Simulation output, which includes: cpu_insns: Total CPU instructions. mem_limit: Peak memory usage. ledger_reads: Number of entries read. ledger_writes: Number of entries written.

To create reproducible results, you must control your environment. Stable Ledger State: Always run benchmarks against a known, pre-populated state. Release Profile: Always build your contract with cargo build --release before measuring. Warm vs. Cold Cache: Note that the first time an entry is read, it costs more than subsequent reads in the same transaction.

Problem: Iterating through a Vec stored in a single storage key to find or update an item. This is O(n) and becomes exponentially more expensive as the collection grows. Before (O(n)) After (O(1)) #[contracttype] pub struct Registry { pub users: Vec<Address>, } // Every time you add a user, you read the WHOLE list, // append, and write the WHOLE list back. pub fn add_user(env: Env, user: Address) { let mut registry: Registry = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Reg).unwrap(); if !registry.users.contains(&user) { registry.users.push_back(user); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Reg, &registry); } } // Use separate keys for each user. pub fn add_user(env: Env, user: Address) { let key = DataKey::User(user.clone()); if !env.storage().persistent().has(&key) { env.storage().persistent().set(&key, &true); } } Impact: Switching to individual keys reduces cpu_insns and ledger_read_bytes linearly with the size of the collection.

Problem: Storing all contract state in one large "monolithic" struct. Updating a single boolean requires reading and writing the entire 1KB+ object. Cost of Monoliths Reading a 2KB struct costs twice as much gas as reading a 1KB struct, even if you only need 1 byte of data from it. Optimization: Split the struct into "hot" (frequently updated) and "cold" (read-only or rarely updated) storage keys.

Problem: Accessing env.storage() multiple times for the same value in a single function call. // ❌ BAD: Multiple reads pub fn do_something(env: Env) { let admin = env.storage().instance().get::<_, Address>(&DataKey::Admin).unwrap(); // ... logic ... let admin_again = env.storage().instance().get::<_, Address>(&DataKey::Admin).unwrap(); } // ✅ GOOD: Read once, pass around pub fn do_something(env: Env) { let admin = env.storage().instance().get::<_, Address>(&DataKey::Admin).unwrap(); Self::internal_logic(&admin); }
If you need to store multiple flags or small numbers, pack them into a single u64 or u128 to save on storage bytes.

Instance Storage: Best for global config (read on every invocation). Persistent Storage: Best for user balances (long-lived, expensive). Temporary Storage: Best for oracles or sequence numbers (cheap, but must be bumped).

When submitting an optimization PR, include a "Before & After" table: Metric Before After Change CPU Instructions 1,200,000 450,000 -62.5% Mem Limit 512 KB 256 KB -50% Wasm Size 12 KB 9 KB -25% Ledger Reads 5 2 -60%

I have established a baseline using soroban contract simulate. I am building with --release for all measurements. I have eliminated O(n) storage patterns (linear scans). I have split large structs to reduce read/write amplification. I have verified the improvement with a follow-up simulation.

The oracle consumer pattern enables smart contracts to read external data (price feeds, asset prices, etc.) from trusted oracle contracts through cross-contract invocation.

An oracle consumer contract: Reads data from an external oracle contract Validates data freshness and accuracy Uses prices for calculations (value estimation, collateral checks) Handles oracle failures gracefully Maintains configurable trust parameters

DEX/AMM: Price feeds for token swaps and liquidity pools Lending Protocols: Collateral valuation and liquidation pricing Staking: Asset price feeds for reward calculations Insurance: Event triggers based on oracle data Derivatives: Price feeds for options and futures

┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Oracle Consumer Contract │ ├─────────────────────────────┤ │ get_price(asset) │ │ get_price_data(asset) │ │ calculate_value(asset, amt) │ │ validate_freshness() │ └──────────┬──────────────────┘ │ Cross-Contract Call │ ┌──────────▼──────────────────┐ │ Oracle Contract │ ├─────────────────────────────┤ │ price_feeds (persistent) │ │ last_update (timestamp) │ │ update_prices() │ └─────────────────────────────┘

Query: Consumer asks oracle for price of asset Fetch: Oracle looks up price from data store Return: Oracle returns price with metadata (decimals, timestamp) Validate: Consumer checks freshness and accuracy Use: Consumer uses validated price for calculations
Oracle Contract: Deployed by trusted party Data Accuracy: Oracle is incentivized to provide accurate prices Timeliness: Oracle updates prices regularly Integrity: Oracle cannot be tampered with

Freshness Checks: Reject stale data beyond max_age Price Bounds: Reject prices outside reasonable ranges Multiple Oracles: Average prices from multiple sources Circuit Breakers: Pause operations if prices are unusual

#[contract] pub struct OracleConsumer; #[contractimpl] impl OracleConsumer { /// Initialize with oracle address and data freshness requirement pub fn init(env: Env, oracle_address: Address, max_age_secs: u64) { env.storage() .instance() .set(&symbol_short!("oracle"), &oracle_address); env.storage() .instance() .set(&symbol_short!("max_age"), &max_age_secs); } /// Fetch price from oracle with validation pub fn get_price(env: Env, asset: Symbol) -> Result<i128, OracleError> { let oracle = env.storage() .instance() .get(&symbol_short!("oracle")) .expect("Oracle not initialized"); // Call oracle contract let price_data: Vec<i128> = env .invoke_contract( &oracle, &symbol_short!("get_price"), soroban_sdk::vec![&env, asset.into_val(&env)], ) .map_err(|_| OracleError::InvalidOracle)?; // Validate response format if price_data.len() < 3 { return Err(OracleError::InvalidPrice); } let price = price_data.get_unchecked(0); let timestamp = price_data.get_unchecked(2) as u64; // Validate price is positive if price <= 0 { return Err(OracleError::InvalidPrice); } // Check data freshness let max_age = env.storage() .instance() .get(&symbol_short!("max_age")) .unwrap_or(3600); let current_time = env.ledger().timestamp(); let age = current_time.checked_sub(timestamp) .ok_or(OracleError::StaleData)?; if age > max_age { return Err(OracleError::StaleData); } Ok(price) } /// Calculate value of amount based on oracle price pub fn calculate_value( env: Env, asset: Symbol, amount: i128, ) -> Result<i128, OracleError> { let (price, decimals, _) = self.get_price_data(env, asset)?; // value = (amount * price) / 10^decimals let value = amount .checked_mul(price) .ok_or(OracleError::InvalidPrice)? .checked_div(10_i128.pow(decimals)) .ok_or(OracleError::InvalidPrice)?; Ok(value) } }

#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)] #[repr(u32)] pub enum OracleError { StaleData = 1, // Data too old InvalidOracle = 2, // Oracle call failed InvalidPrice = 3, // Price is invalid Unauthorized = 4, // Not authorized }

The oracle consumer includes comprehensive tests with a mock oracle: #[contract] pub struct MockOracle; #[contractimpl] impl MockOracle { pub fn get_price(env: Env, asset: Symbol) -> Vec<i128> { // Return: [price, decimals, timestamp] soroban_sdk::vec![ &env, 1_000_000, // $1.00 6, // 6 decimals env.ledger().timestamp() as i128, // current time ] } } #[test] fn test_get_price() { let env = Env::default(); let consumer_id = env.register_contract(None, OracleConsumer); let oracle_id = env.register_contract(None, MockOracle); let client = OracleConsumerClient::new(&env, &consumer_id); client.init(&oracle_id, &3600); let price = client.get_price(&Symbol::new(&env, "USD")).unwrap(); assert_eq!(price, 1_000_000); } #[test] fn test_stale_data_rejection() { let env = Env::default(); // ... setup ... // Advance time beyond max_age env.ledger_mut().set_timestamp(old_timestamp + 7200); let result = client.get_price(&Symbol::new(&env, "USD")); assert_eq!(result, Err(OracleError::StaleData)); }
Always validate timestamp and reject stale data: let max_age = 3600; // 1 hour let age = current_time - timestamp; if age > max_age { return Err(OracleError::StaleData); }
Reject prices outside reasonable ranges: // BTC price between $10k and $100k if price < 10_000_000_000 || price > 100_000_000_000 { return Err(OracleError::InvalidPrice); }

Use multiple oracles to prevent single point of failure: pub fn get_median_price(env: Env, asset: Symbol) -> Result<i128, OracleError> { let mut prices = Vec::new(); for oracle_addr in self.get_oracles(&env)? { if let Ok(price) = self.fetch_from_oracle(&env, &oracle_addr, &asset) { prices.push(price); } } if prices.is_empty() { return Err(OracleError::InvalidOracle); } // Return median to handle outliers prices.sort(); Ok(prices[prices.len() / 2]) }

Handle oracle failures gracefully: pub fn get_price_or_cached( env: Env, asset: Symbol, ) -> Result<i128, OracleError> { // Try fresh price match self.get_price(&env, &asset) { Ok(price) => { // Cache for fallback self.cache_price(&env, &asset, price)?; Ok(price) } Err(_) => { // Fall back to cached price if oracle fails self.get_cached_price(&env, &asset) } } }

Restrict configuration changes to authorized addresses: pub fn set_oracle(env: Env, new_oracle: Address) { let admin: Address = env.storage() .instance() .get(&symbol_short!("admin")) .expect("Admin not set"); require_auth(&admin); env.storage() .instance() .set(&symbol_short!("oracle"), &new_oracle); }

Handle different decimal places: pub fn normalize_price(price: i128, decimals: u32, target_decimals: u32) -> i128 { if decimals > target_decimals { price / 10_i128.pow(decimals - target_decimals) } else { price * 10_i128.pow(target_decimals - decimals) } }

Calculate asset value from price and amount: pub fn calculate_usd_value( price: i128, // Price in USD decimals: u32, // Price decimals amount: i128, // Amount of asset amount_decimals: u32, // Asset decimals ) -> Result<i128, OracleError> { // Normalize to same decimal place let price_normalized = normalize_price(price, decimals, amount_decimals); // value = amount * price / 10^decimals let value = amount .checked_mul(price_normalized) .ok_or(OracleError::InvalidPrice)? .checked_div(10_i128.pow(amount_decimals)) .ok_or(OracleError::InvalidPrice)?; Ok(value) }

Pause operations if price changes dramatically: pub fn check_circuit_breaker( env: Env, asset: Symbol, new_price: i128, ) -> Result<(), OracleError> { let old_price = self.get_cached_price(&env, &asset)?; // Allow max 20% price change let max_deviation = old_price / 5; let deviation = (new_price as i128 - old_price).abs(); if deviation > max_deviation { return Err(OracleError::PriceDeviation); } Ok(()) }

Risk: Oracle goes offline, contract uses stale prices Mitigation: Set reasonable max_age (typically 1 hour) Monitor oracle update frequency Use circuit breakers for unusual price changes Fall back to cached prices
Risk: Oracle provides false prices Mitigation: Use multiple independent oracle sources Verify oracle is properly incentivized/bonded Implement price bounds checking Monitor for suspicious patterns

Risk: Malicious oracle contract returns crafted data Mitigation: Whitelist oracle addresses Validate response format and types Use safe math (checked_mul, checked_div) Test with multiple data scenarios
Risk: Oracle takes excessive gas or fails unexpectedly Mitigation: Set gas limits on oracle calls Implement timeouts Use try/catch for failure scenarios Fall back to cached prices

Trust Dependency: Consumer trusts oracle's data accuracy Availability: Relies on oracle being online Latency: Data is never completely real-time Cost: Oracle calls consume gas Manipulation: Oracles can be attacked or compromised

Governance contracts need a clear, auditable state machine so that proposals can only advance through valid transitions. This pattern encodes the full lifecycle as a #[contracttype] enum and enforces transitions at the contract boundary, making invalid states unrepresentable on-chain. Pending ──► Active ──► Succeeded ──► Executed └──► Defeated Prerequisites Rust stable and cargo Soroban CLI installed (setup guide) Familiarity with contracttype enums and instance storage Implementation Design principle Encode every invalid state as a compile-time impossibility or a guarded assert!. Never rely on callers to pass the right state — the contract should enforce it. Contract Tests #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, contracttype, Env}; /// All valid proposal states. #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, PartialEq, Debug)] pub enum ProposalState { Pending, // created but voting not open Active, // voting is open Succeeded, // more for-votes than against Defeated, // equal or more against-votes Executed, // on-chain action has been carried out } #[contracttype] pub enum DataKey { State, VotesFor, VotesAgainst, } #[contract] pub struct SimpleDao; #[contractimpl] impl SimpleDao { /// Create a new proposal in the Pending state. pub fn create(env: Env) { env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &ProposalState::Pending); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::VotesFor, &0_u32); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::VotesAgainst, &0_u32); } /// Pending → Active: open voting. pub fn activate(env: Env) { let state: ProposalState = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap(); assert!(state == ProposalState::Pending, "must be Pending to activate"); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &ProposalState::Active); } /// Record a vote while Active. pub fn vote(env: Env, in_favor: bool) { let state: ProposalState = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap(); assert!(state == ProposalState::Active, "voting is not open"); if in_favor { let v: u32 = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::VotesFor).unwrap_or(0); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::VotesFor, &(v + 1)); } else { let v: u32 = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::VotesAgainst).unwrap_or(0); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::VotesAgainst, &(v + 1)); } } /// Active → Succeeded or Defeated based on vote counts. pub fn finalize(env: Env) { let state: ProposalState = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap(); assert!(state == ProposalState::Active, "must be Active to finalize"); let for_votes: u32 = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::VotesFor).unwrap_or(0); let against_votes: u32 = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::VotesAgainst).unwrap_or(0); let next = if for_votes > against_votes { ProposalState::Succeeded } else { ProposalState::Defeated }; env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &next); } /// Succeeded → Executed: carry out the on-chain action. pub fn execute(env: Env) { let state: ProposalState = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap(); assert!(state == ProposalState::Succeeded, "must be Succeeded to execute"); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &ProposalState::Executed); } pub fn get_state(env: Env) -> ProposalState { env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap() } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::Env; fn setup() -> (Env, soroban_sdk::Address) { let env = Env::default(); let id = env.register(SimpleDao, ()); (env, id) } #[test] fn test_create_sets_pending() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Pending); } #[test] fn test_pending_to_active() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Active); } #[test] fn test_active_to_succeeded() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); client.vote(&true); client.vote(&true); client.vote(&false); client.finalize(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Succeeded); } #[test] fn test_active_to_defeated() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); client.vote(&false); client.vote(&false); client.vote(&true); client.finalize(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Defeated); } #[test] fn test_succeeded_to_executed() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); client.vote(&true); client.finalize(); client.execute(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Executed); } #[test] #[should_panic(expected = "must be Pending to activate")] fn test_cannot_activate_twice() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); client.activate(); // invalid } #[test] #[should_panic(expected = "voting is not open")] fn test_cannot_vote_when_pending() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.vote(&true); // invalid } #[test] #[should_panic(expected = "must be Succeeded to execute")] fn test_cannot_execute_defeated_proposal() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); client.vote(&false); client.finalize(); client.execute(); // invalid } } Security considerations Authorization: Production DAOs must guard activate, finalize, and execute with require_auth() on a governor address or multi-sig. The example omits this for clarity. Tie handling: The current rule (for > against) treats ties as defeats. Make this explicit in your governance spec. Double execution: Once Executed, the state cannot regress. Add any further idempotency guards inside the execute body. Sybil resistance: Vote weighting (token-weighted, NFT-gated) must be added before production use. Production checklist Add require_auth() guards on every privileged transition before deploying to mainnet. A timelock vault locks an asset amount on-chain until a specific Unix timestamp. Only after that timestamp can the beneficiary withdraw the funds. The depositor may cancel before unlock to recover their assets.
Vesting schedules (e.g. lock team tokens for 12 months) Escrow with a time-based release trigger Scheduled payments / grant disbursements Time-delayed multi-sig safety nets

deposit(depositor, beneficiary, amount, unlock_time) └─ stores vault data; reverts if already initialised or inputs invalid withdraw() └─ releases funds to beneficiary; reverts if still locked or already claimed cancel() └─ depositor reclaims funds; only valid before unlock_time unlock_time() / amount() / beneficiary() / time_remaining() / is_claimed() └─ read-only view helpers

Key Type Storage Description Depositor Address persistent Account that locked the funds Beneficiary Address persistent Account allowed to withdraw after lock Amount i128 persistent Token amount locked (stroops) UnlockTime u64 persistent Unix timestamp (seconds) for release Claimed bool persistent Whether vault has been claimed/cancelled persistent storage ensures the vault survives ledger TTL expiry without manual extension.

examples/timelock-vault/src/lib.rs #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contracterror, contractimpl, contracttype, Address, Env}; #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone)] pub enum DataKey { Depositor, Beneficiary, Amount, UnlockTime, Claimed, } #[contracterror] #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Ord)] #[repr(u32)] pub enum Error { AlreadyInitialised = 1, NotInitialised = 2, NotUnlockedYet = 3, AlreadyClaimed = 4, Unauthorised = 5, InvalidAmount = 6, InvalidUnlockTime = 7, } #[contract] pub struct TimelockVault; #[contractimpl] impl TimelockVault { pub fn deposit( env: Env, depositor: Address, beneficiary: Address, amount: i128, unlock_time: u64, ) -> Result<(), Error> { depositor.require_auth(); if env.storage().persistent().has(&DataKey::Depositor) { return Err(Error::AlreadyInitialised); } if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } if unlock_time <= env.ledger().timestamp() { return Err(Error::InvalidUnlockTime); } env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Depositor, &depositor); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Beneficiary, &beneficiary); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Amount, &amount); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::UnlockTime, &unlock_time); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Claimed, &false); Ok(()) } pub fn withdraw(env: Env) -> Result<i128, Error> { Self::assert_initialised(&env)?; if env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::Claimed).unwrap_or(false) { return Err(Error::AlreadyClaimed); } let unlock_time: u64 = env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::UnlockTime).unwrap(); if env.ledger().timestamp() < unlock_time { return Err(Error::NotUnlockedYet); } let amount: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::Amount).unwrap(); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Claimed, &true); Ok(amount) } pub fn cancel(env: Env) -> Result<i128, Error> { Self::assert_initialised(&env)?; let depositor: Address = env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::Depositor).unwrap(); depositor.require_auth(); if env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::Claimed).unwrap_or(false) { return Err(Error::AlreadyClaimed); } let unlock_time: u64 = env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::UnlockTime).unwrap(); if env.ledger().timestamp() >= unlock_time { return Err(Error::Unauthorised); } let amount: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::Amount).unwrap(); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Claimed, &true); Ok(amount) } pub fn unlock_time(env: Env) -> Result<u64, Error> { Self::assert_initialised(&env)?; Ok(env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::UnlockTime).unwrap()) } pub fn amount(env: Env) -> Result<i128, Error> { Self::assert_initialised(&env)?; Ok(env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::Amount).unwrap()) } pub fn is_claimed(env: Env) -> bool { env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::Claimed).unwrap_or(false) } pub fn beneficiary(env: Env) -> Result<Address, Error> { Self::assert_initialised(&env)?; Ok(env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::Beneficiary).unwrap()) } pub fn time_remaining(env: Env) -> Result<u64, Error> { Self::assert_initialised(&env)?; let unlock_time: u64 = env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::UnlockTime).unwrap(); let now = env.ledger().timestamp(); Ok(if now >= unlock_time { 0 } else { unlock_time - now }) } fn assert_initialised(env: &Env) -> Result<(), Error> { if !env.storage().persistent().has(&DataKey::Depositor) { return Err(Error::NotInitialised); } Ok(()) } }

Claimed is set to true before returning the amount in both withdraw and cancel. This prevents re-entrancy even though Soroban's execution model already guards against it at the host level — the pattern makes the intent explicit.
Vault state must survive beyond a single ledger bump window. persistent storage entries have an independent TTL that can be extended, making them appropriate for long-duration locks (months/years).

cancel calls depositor.require_auth() so the depositor's signature must be present in the transaction's authorisation tree. This prevents a third party from prematurely cancelling a vault on behalf of the depositor.

This contract records amounts but does not move tokens directly — it is intentionally scoped as a basic vault to demonstrate the time-lock pattern without the additional complexity of SAC (Stellar Asset Contract) integration. See the token-transfer example for cross-contract token movement.
